game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I think I got this for free some months ago and now got to play it. It ran rather fine on an Ubuntu 18.04 lapttop with Nouveau drivers, game has native Linux support. 
You play as a worker for a surveillance program, sorting through the web and accessing peoples devices, looking for clues about terrorists. I cant really compare the game to anything, maybe it is similar to a graphical novel to some extent, as you have limited choices, but you do have to use your head, even if the game pretty much always at least tells you where to look for clues.  
It was almost an initimate experience to look into the character life, their private chats and calls. I feel like they could have added a bit more "useless" webpages, to make the game more authentic, but it is obvious that they tried  to give their characters depth, which is where the game shines. 
As the name of the game tells us, to some extent it is obviously a political/ethical game, even if done rather abstract (you work for "the nation", and pretty much everyone you investigate did something wrong). 
One thing I really appreciated, was that they show what can happen if systems like this make mistakes, which is something I feel like is not discussed enough as a counterargument to surveillance, besides the obvious ethical ones.  Overall the the game is an interesting experience, but not comparable to games like "Spec Ops -  The Line", where you really have to get your hands dirty, which lessens the impression of consequences of the players actions in my opinion.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Wow. 3 Episodes in, and I'm hooked. Will go into some detail in a moment, but let me start this with a warning:

If you play this game: TAKE. YOUR. TIME.
Don't power through it. Read everything. Let the narrative grab you, pull you in.
Then step away. For a day, perhaps two.
The episodes come out once a week -- and that gives you quite a bit of time to reflect on what you discovered, as well as the potential consequences of your actions.

That said, you'll read some reviews here that weigh heavily on the feelings that the game is effectively "on rails", and as a result this lends a very shallow narrative. Being that most of those were placed during only the first or second episode, of five, that's rather short-sighted. That being said, the narrative is NOT quick, and there is quite a bit to it that presumes you're going to fill in some of the holes. If you need full action to enjoy a game, this may not be a good fit for you.

Overall, Purely Subjective Score: 4.25/5

Storyline: 4/5
I've got a few quibbles. There are aspects to the story that are a bit too on the nose at times, pushing forward the big-brother aspect of the narrative, but overall, the slow burn aspect of the storyline as a whole is compelling. Despite that much of it is scripted, to the point that I really think that much of the illusion of control on the part of the player is exactly that -- an illusion, it doesn't take away from the overall story being told. You are a cog in the big mahcine that is Big Brother, in a far-more Orwellian nation-state, and you're taken on for the ride.

Art: 3/5
The art style here is exactly what is shown on the tin -- and while it gives the game a strange noir flavor, but there are aspects to it that are very displeasing from a purely aesthetic standpoint. I think it's mostly that it places me back in the days of heavy, visible polygon use in old games, which I'm frankly glad we've moved away from.

Verisimiltude: 3/5
This is fiction, pure and simple, but there are aspects to the tech that seems very magic/hand-wavey. I find myself wishing there was a bit more legitimacy to the tech you're supposed to be using.

Replayability: 4.5/5
There are a few mechanics within gameplay that are integral in giving the feeling that actions have consequences, and impact on the narrative. Some are small, others more significant (which I can't descibe without spoilers). Some details you highlight in-game are 'pointless' fluff, others can give the wrong (or right) perspective on a subject's motivations, and yet others can be clear conflicts in data that you have to choose between. All frame and connect the narrative. In some cases, this can lead to crimes being prevented (or not), people dying (or not), or the right/wrong accusation coming out in an interrogation. Remembering those, and seeing what happens if you go another route, can potentially lend to some completionist replays.

Overall? I encourage you to check this one out.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell: Keeping An Eye On You (in short, Orwell) is a five-part episodic narrative-driven mystery video game by Osmotic Studios set in a dystopian world in which the player assumes the role of a governmental operative who monitors surveillance sources to discovery national security threats. The game is named after the famed anti-totalitarian writer George Orwell and is inspired by themes established by his magnum opus novel, 1984.

The story in Orwell takes place in a country named The Nation which is governed by a contemporary authoritarian government known as The Party. Due to a series of events in the past, The Party passed the Safety Bill which expanded the government's capability to spy on its citizens in the name of national security. To accomplish this, the Ministry of Security, at the helm of Secretary of Security Catherine Delacroix, built a secret surveillance system codenamed Orwell. After a successful application and being selected from a pool of candidates, the player takes the role of an outsourced Orwell investigator who lives outside The Nation and is tasked, with the help of an assigned advisor going by the alias of Symes, to find evidence on the terrorist (individual or group) who caused a bomb explosion during a presumably peaceful protest in the populated Freedom Plaza in Bonton, the capital city of The Nation, destroying a statue and killing several people. The player soon stumbles upon an activist group called Thought who advocates for freedom of speech with anti-governmental sentiments, yet unaware of Orwell, who is entangled in the bombing incident. From there on, the player uses everything at their disposal to find evidence to expectantly incriminate their first suspect, Cassandra Watergate, an artist who was present at the Plaza shortly before the explosion.

The story occurs across five days (episodes) and what originally seemed like another day at the office, turns into an intricate roller-coaster of a journey full of conspiracy theories, deception and shocking revelations. The narrative in Orwell is exceptionally well-written and what keeps the player on their toes and constantly engaged. Just as things might get slightly monotonous now and again, the story always seems to throw you a new bone through unexpected plot twists and interestingly branched out paths shaped by your various choices and consequences. Even though the story occurs across a country, Orwell actually focuses on a small group of individuals despite the illusion it might give in the beginning, thus I did end up wishing more citizens were actually involved in the end. Whilst this is somewhat disappointing, it makes for a more focused story and does help to get better attached to those said characters, which Orwell succeeds in both aspects. Frankly, the overarching story and its thought-provoking themes, along with the interesting characters you encounter along your journey, albeit a touch stereotypical once in a while, are the selling points of Orwell, and I am delighted to report that it satisfied my itch for a robust adventure mystery game which I have not had for a while recently. Due to the nature of the game, I cannot talk more about the story nor discuss its outcomes at this point, as it is best to unravel and experience it yourself, but there are about four confirmed endings. The game’s length lies somewhere between 4 – 6 hours, which I personally completed in one sitting thanks to its captivating story which made me impatiently want to know what happens next, but I do wish it were longer.

All in all, Orwell's gameplay is akin to a visual novel, so there is not a lot of interactivity involved, but what it does, mechanically speaking, is very solid and straightforward. During investigations, the player has to do various tasks such as (1) browsing and reading through news articles, social media pages and databases, (2) hacking computers or mobile phones to access stored data, and (3) wiretapping conversations over the phone and messaging applications. Each one of these tasks displays various text passages in the form of datachuncks (highlighted by the game for the player’s ease) which could be uploaded on the surveillance system to piece together clues, construct evidence on suspects and, in theory, incriminate them. Each new datachunck uploaded updates a suspect’s profile with more information and occasionally even opens up profiles of new suspects in connection to the respective suspect as the plot thickens. You cannot undo an upload, so think carefully beforehand. Sometimes suspects give contradicting statements over the duration of the story through either dishonesty or unintended misinformation as the result of human nature, which you would then have to use your own judgement and decide which datachunck to upload to support the government’s case, or not. You see, the player can play by the rules to appease the government or ignore vital information to protect the suspects (depending on your moral compass), and either playstyle has several cleverly written consequences. The mechanics do feel too simplistic and repetitive but begin to shine in the second half of the game once there is a lot more information to chew and digest. Moreover, the adviser gives you bite-sized info as to what is happening during almost each one of your moves, so technically you should not feel lost with how the story unfolds. Plus, at the end of each day, a window summary displays all your findings and events that occurred on the day to be up to speed.

One major criticism I do have with its gameplay, however, is that despite the game warning the player that they are not required to upload every datachunk spotted, I always had the compulsion to upload everything I could find regardless since there is no penalty for doing so as far as I recall, aside for a handful of contradictions and, of course, the path of some key plot events. Retrospectively, I feel the game should have better incentivised the player to upload fewer datachuncks or increased contradictions to spice things up. Unfortunately, the game limits your number datachuncks uploads to create a nerve-wracking atmosphere (commendable mechanic) only at the end and I wish that was predominant throughout the entire game instead.

Visually, Orwell is all about the graphical user interface (of a computer monitor) since that is where you will be carrying out all your investigations and decision-making. The art style with its stylized polygonal pictures suits its dystopian themes and the presentation is sufficiently appealing thanks to its good use of appropriate colour pallets and well-designed page layouts. The interface is also intuitive and easy to navigate as a result of its slick design. Whilst the soundtrack is rather short and may seem minimal, it brilliantly captures the eerie atmosphere and even gets momentarily tenser when a plot twist occurs and stakes have risen. Considering there is plenty of reading and no voice acting involved, the tone and vibe of the soundtrack help it to never become distracting.

In conclusion, Orwell: Keeping An Eye On You is a fantastic, but short, mystery game set in a frightfully believable dystopian setting with a strong narrative that challenges your own ethics and presents balanced points of view in the long-lasting battle between the individual’s freedom and privacy versus the government’s security and surveillance. Whilst it is mechanically simplistic and not as diverse, nor challenging, as a game like Papers Please which shares a few familiar social commentaries, it is unique in its own right and worthy of a spiritual successor to 1984. At the end of the day, it is an interactive book more than a conventional adventure game where you might solve puzzles, which feels appropriate considering it is inspired by a novel. Definitely a must-play for George Orwell fans like myself and anyone interested in good mystery/detective games in the format of visual novels.

Stay vigilant.

review_text_raw:
[h1] An Excellent Educational Tool for Teaching People the Value of Privacy [/h1]

I am going to start this review with a hot take: people don't care much about privacy. At least not in the way we're taught to think about it. People desire privacy when they want to hide from others—especially people they know. A classic example of this is your average teenager concealing their sexual activity from their parents. We can define this as [b]interpersonal privacy[/b]—the need and right to keep parts of ourselves hidden from the people around us. In a limited sense, people do care about having (intepersonal) privacy  in their lives. 

But what about a faceless entity like a government agency or a big tech company? Should we seek privacy from their probing eyes? Do we even deserve the right to privacy from the government and Big Tech? This is precisely where people will shrug their shoulders and say that they don't understand or care. Interpersonal privacy matters to the common man. Privacy from institutions and systems does not.

Why are we like this? The reasons for this range from the righteous to the fearful to the misguided.

[list]
[*] Fear: A citizen concerned for their safety will give up essential liberty as Ben Franklin pointed out. This was evident after the Patriot Act was passed. It was evident again after the Snowden leaks. People feel like they will be safe from violent crime if they give up rights. As Franklin rightly noted, this safety is but temporary. It is futile to give up your rights to secure it.
[*] Righteousness: Many people use the 'nothing to hide' fallacy to justify the lack of privacy. People will say that they are not criminals. And so, they have nothing to hide from the government. This righteousness is misguided because it is based on the presumption that governments are always righteous and have the best intentions for their subjects. Governments can and do turn tyrannical—when they do, they spy on and punish citizens.
[*] Ignorance (of consequence): People do not understand how much private information the government and BIg Tech has about them. Information is power—this is especially true in the age of data. Information about you can be used to easily understand and manipulate you. But people do not understand how private information is collected and misused. And so they don't care about privacy. [/list]

Educating people about the need for, let alone the right to privacy is a challenging task. We need to reframe and redirect the conversation away from interpersonal privacy to privacy from insitutions. Doing this is difficult because institutional surveillance feels like an abstract concept to many. This is precisely where the game Orwell excels. Osmotic Studios does a great job of showing why your life should be private from the government and Big Tech. In Orwell, you play as a government agent snooping on ordinary citizens. You gather personal information for a surveillance system designed to store data and weaponize it. Every piece of information you harvest is used to create damaging narratives, justify injustice and enable tyranny. The net result of your gameplay is acutely felt on a personal level. Your actions lead to individuals being maligned, families torn apart and the world becoming worse.

Orwell is thus a great educational tool for privacy advocates looking to teach the public about the value of and the right to privacy.

[h1] Recommendations for Specific Gamers [/h1]

[h2] Voyeuristic & Paranoid Gamers [/h2]
[list]
[*] Do you lie in bed with your partner, look at him and think to yourself: "I bet he's thinking about other women."
[*] Do you spy on your loving girlfriend's phone because you constantly suspect her of using dating apps?
[*] Are you a chai enthusiast who loves to talk about tea with other women on Tea apps?
[*] Or perhaps you are a masculine married man who revels in the simple joys of candaulism?
[/list]

If you answered yes to any of these questions, you must play Orwell! The game is a voyeur's delight. It will scratch every voyeuristic itch—and trust issues—that you have.

[h2] Gamers Who Love to Gaslight & Manipulate [/h2]
Orwell not only allows you to spy on people but also to shape the narrative about them. Do you want a woman to be seen as a loving single mom who dotes on her child? Or do you want her to be seen as a mentally unstable terrorist who commits violence? You have the power to choose in Orwell! 

This ability to manipulate and shape narratives is one of the best gameplay mechanics in Orwell. You can gaslight the government itself into believing what you want them to believe! Wonderful! This is exactly why video games appeal to the male fantasy!

Bottom line:  I cared too much about getting things right while playing Orwell. But the game doesn't want you to do that! In fact, creating a false narrative about NPC characters is required for some achievements. So yeah, don't worry too much. Go ahead and play fast and loose with the truth!

[h2] 1984 Enjoyers [/h2]
Let's get this straight: Orwell is a great tool to teach people about privacy. But it is no literary masterpeice. Yes the game pays homage to 1984. But Orwell treads familiar ground about liberty, security and privacy. It is not designed to be a sophisticated commentary on the issues and concepts it deals with.

That said, I loved the character of Abraham Goldfels. He is a fascinating case study of a person who is co-opted by the very surveillance state he is trying to fight. Abraham is a complicated character with ambiguous motivations. I started the game feeling a sense of admiration for his intellectual nature and ability to lead. I ended the game feeling conflicted about his past and his life choices. What do you think of Abraham? Leave a message in the comments sections if you'd like to talk about him!

[h2] Reading Haters [/h2]
Orwell is a text heavy game. You will be reading and analyzing articles, chat logs, documents, emails and much more. For those who love reading books, Orwell is an enjoyable game. But those who dislike reading will struggle.

My eyes did sometimes glaze over the many walls of text I went through. Fortuntately, the plot and gameplay is engaging enough to sustain you through. The first episode feels sluggish as you learn the ropes of the game. But keep at it: Orwell gets a lot more interesting in the later acts.

[h2] Atmospheric Music Enjoyers [/h2]
Orwell's soundtrack is definitely vibey. The slow and atmospheric music gets you in the mood of being a detective who is investigating criminal cases. Not a music critic so I can't say more than that.

[h2] Achievement/Completionist Hunters [/h2]
The game is not too hard for achievement hunters and completionists. Multiple playthroughs are not needed. You only need to replay some episodes to get specific achievements. I recommend [url=https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=907778579] using this achievement guide [/url] which helped me get 100%.

Warning: Orwell is buggy and suffers from major save file issues. Backing up game files will not help IMO because of the persistent autosave feature. The first time I played Orwell, I lost progress and so I quit playing. The second time around, I finished the game and then bounced between chapters to get the remaining achievements. Once again, the game tripped up and asked me to replay the game from scratch!

My advice is to play through the game once. Then check which achievements you need and which episodes they fall in. Need achievements for Episodes 4 & 5? Replay [b] those episodes first in chronological order [/b]. If necessary, repeat the episodes until you get all the episode specific achievements.

For Episodes 1-3, I recommend creating a [b] separate profile [/b] and then playing the episodes in order. Episode 3 in particular is a mess because you have to replay it 3 times at least to get the achievements! 

[h1] Overall Rating [/h1]
[b] WIP, FIS, IIS
2+2=5/6 [/b]

Your actions lead to individuals being maligned, families torn apart and the world becoming worse. Orwell is thus a great educational tool for privacy advocates looking to teach the public about the value of and the right to privacy. [h1] Recommendations for Specific Gamers [/h1] [h2] Voyeuristic & Paranoid Gamers [/h2] [list] [*] Do you lie in bed with your partner, look at him and think to yourself: "I bet he's thinking about other women." [*] Do you spy on your loving girlfriend's phone because you constantly suspect her of using dating apps? [*] Are you a chai enthusiast who loves to talk about tea with other women on Tea apps? [*] Or perhaps you are a masculine married man who revels in the simple joys of candaulism? [/list] If you answered yes to any of these questions, you must play Orwell! The game is a voyeur's delight. It will scratch every voyeuristic itch—and trust issues—that you have. [h2] Gamers Who Love to Gaslight & Manipulate [/h2] Orwell not only allows you to spy on people but also to shape the narrative about them. Do you want a woman to be seen as a loving single mom who dotes on her child? Or do you want her to be seen as a mentally unstable terrorist who commits violence? You have the power to choose in Orwell! This ability to manipulate and shape narratives is one of the best gameplay mechanics in Orwell. You can gaslight the government itself into believing what you want them to believe! Wonderful! This is exactly why video games appeal to the male fantasy! Bottom line: I cared too much about getting things right while playing Orwell. But the game doesn't want you to do that! In fact, creating a false narrative about NPC characters is required for some achievements. So yeah, don't worry too much. Go ahead and play fast and loose with the truth! [h2] 1984 Enjoyers [/h2] Let's get this straight: Orwell is a great tool to teach people about privacy. But it is no literary masterpeice. Yes the game pays homage to 1984. But Orwell treads familiar ground about liberty, security and privacy. It is not designed to be a sophisticated commentary on the issues and concepts it deals with. That said, I loved the character of Abraham Goldfels. He is a fascinating case study of a person who is co-opted by the very surveillance state he is trying to fight. Abraham is a complicated character with ambiguous motivations. I started the game feeling a sense of admiration for his intellectual nature and ability to lead. I ended the game feeling conflicted about his past and his life choices. What do you think of Abraham? Leave a message in the comments sections if you'd like to talk about him! [h2] Reading Haters [/h2] Orwell is a text heavy game. You will be reading and analyzing articles, chat logs, documents, emails and much more. For those who love reading books, Orwell is an enjoyable game. But those who dislike reading will struggle. My eyes did sometimes glaze over the many walls of text I went through. Fortuntately, the plot and gameplay is engaging enough to sustain you through. The first episode feels sluggish as you learn the ropes of the game. But keep at it: Orwell gets a lot more interesting in the later acts. [h2] Atmospheric Music Enjoyers [/h2] Orwell's soundtrack is definitely vibey. The slow and atmospheric music gets you in the mood of being a detective who is investigating criminal cases. Not a music critic so I can't say more than that. [h2] Achievement/Completionist Hunters [/h2] The game is not too hard for achievement hunters and completionists. Multiple playthroughs are not needed. You only need to replay some episodes to get specific achievements. I recommend [url=https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=907778579] using this achievement guide [/url] which helped me get 100%. Warning: Orwell is buggy and suffers from major save file issues. Backing up game files will not help IMO because of the persistent autosave feature. The first time I played Orwell, I lost progress and so I quit playing. The second time around, I finished the game and then bounced between chapters to get the remaining achievements. Once again, the game tripped up and asked me to replay the game from scratch! My advice is to play through the game once. Then check which achievements you need and which episodes they fall in. Need achievements for Episodes 4 & 5? Replay [b] those episodes first in chronological order [/b]. If necessary, repeat the episodes until you get all the episode specific achievements. For Episodes 1-3, I recommend creating a [b] separate profile [/b] and then playing the episodes in order. Episode 3 in particular is a mess because you have to replay it 3 times at least to get the achievements! [h1] Overall Rating [/h1] [b] WIP, FIS, IIS 2+2=5/6 [/b]

review_text_raw:
Wow I am more than impressed with this game. I am a big fan of the game genre of "Papers, Please", "This is the police" and similar games. I think when games explore your morals and hits you right in your cognitive dissonance. This game does this incredibly well. Surveilence is a difficult subject. There are pros and cons that vary between people.

This game sets your objective as having you aid in finding the suspect for a terrorist attack. This is of course a justifiable action and is in good favor for the public. You quickly start having conflicting thoughts about whether the people you're spying on and the information you gather is relevant at all. I am the type of person who is really interested in other people's affairs. This game absolutely worked wonders on this quirk of mine because I found it difficult to resist to look deeper in people's personal lives. I bet you will too constantly convince yourself that "this guy's past relationship drama might prove useful later".

The writing in this game is absolutely amazing in my honest opinion. This game felt real. The information layout, news articles, blogs, emails, texts, calls all felt real. The way you quickly progress from getting basic information on one person such as their name and occupation suddenly turns into having direct sneaky access to their desktop files, bank account activity and search history. You will find a lot of surprises in this game and lots of VERY difficult choices. There is a lot of conflicting ideas this game forces on you. For example you are presented with 2 or 3 very contradicting pieces of information. Sometimes it is easy to choose based on the source of where this info came from but when the consequences are severe, you are under pressure to make the right choice as there is no going back.

One downfall of this game is that there are some slight errors in the scripting that messes up the flow. For example there are certain bits which I suppose are meant to be discovered in a certain sequence but its possible to do it in the wrong sequence, resulting in dialogue that doesn't fit in. Alerting the higher ups of a threat after it already happened results in them thanking you for the useful information and that they will be prepared...even though this happened just recently and they were not prepared. The game also decides on itself which information is relevant or not and kind of makes you feel bad for collecting everything you might feel is necessary but thankfully you are not outright punished for it. Another big error I noticed was with relationships. I find out that a character has been married in the past and add it to the database but the database instead labels the character as currently married which is considered as wrong information until you find out more details later.

All in all these negatives do not affect the game much. This game is worth full price and I think is a must buy with a discount.

review_text_raw:
Pros:
- The game brings awareness to important social problems: surveillance and totalitarianism
- Music is OK
- The characters are relatable
- Story is realistic
- This implementation of mass surveillance is plausible


Cons:
- Lack of depth in decision. The game is basically linear, except the ending which is a binary moral choice. No replay value.
- Lack of immersion stemming from weak game mechanics.
- The conflict system makes no sense and works against realisticity. How in the world can the system predict that something is in conflict with an unknown data chunk? A conflict should only be shown when both data chunks are known. 
- Phone calls wait for you to tap, such as everything in this game. No time pressure or feeling of urgency.
- The web is way too small, and computer hacking is way too minimalistic to be plausible.
- The enjoyment as you progress is almost a total downward slope. I think the last episode and the ending is just not ready.
- Game lasts no more than 8 hours.

review_text_raw:
Short version: makes you do Important Choices With Consequences based on very little, very shaky, third hand info. Not fun or challenging or possible to engage with sincerely.

Long version: early in the first ep, during what you might call the tutorial, you are asked to choose between two versions of the truth: that a crime suspect was released and case closed because of A) lack of evidence or B) bribes. You are given no context for this choice other than a news article stating that the official version is A but some people think it might be B. I'm not exaggerating. All you have to go on is the word of a journalist you don't know, reporting the words of other people you don't know regarding an incident you just heard of. Even so the game stresses that anything you report will be taken as The Truth and there will be no possibility to undo the choice.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I just finished this game. I like many of the latest reviews received this as part of a humble bundle. Unlike many of the reviewers I am no stranger to the concept of interactive fiction. As such I cannot say "WOW so unique." This game has many elements I found fascinating, and indeed I played through the whole thing in one go, a very do-able task. I think there are many things that would make me recommend it, but there are two glaring holes that I think bring it just shy of a general recommendation. I can say this, If you have never played an interactive fiction game, and the plot sounds intriguing, buy it. It is worth ten dollars. If you got it in a humble bundle or something similar, play it. You will have an entertaining few hours. If you do not fall in to either of those two camps I would recommend a pass. 

The good - 
Plot- Everything to do with the plot is great. The characters are interesting, and they do to some degree develop. The world feels complete and well rounded, The plot is where this game shines, as it should be as interactive fiction lives and dies by the plot. 
The interface - For the most part is pretty solid. There are few idiosyncrasies. The one glaring hole is the need for a few hot-keys, if only Enter and ESC, would make this much easier on the wrists, but it is as a whole soundly usable. 

The bad - For the bad I will go in to detail as to hopefully explain my point of view fully to the Devs.  There is at least one more season planned, and I would love to play it. Perhaps the Devs will hear this feedback and consider it. Before I continue though, if you have already thought “I kinda want to play this game,” do it and forget the ramblings of an old gamer. 

Choice - If the plot is what an interactive fiction game lives and dies by then choice (or for that matter the illusion of choice) is what allows it to breath. In Orwell the idea of choice dies very quickly, and never returns. There are several pivotal moments which finds the player, through the narrative, put in a position to make a pivotal choice. All the relevant characters are obviously pointing at you and saying you decide. I never really felt like there was any choices to be made. Either The player is not given enough context to understand the consequences of that choice, in these cases you are just blindly choosing one of two options and made to accept the consequences. Or you cannot progress until you make the choice. 

At the heart of this, in my opinion, is the engine for which you as the player progress through the narrative. You are told at the very beginning of the game that you cannot progress until you have uploaded certain information. Which pieces of information allows for progression is up to the game. The premise of games like this in which it is up to the player to provide or not provide information to the antagonist is a great juxtaposition to make the player feel invested, and in many cases responsible for the consequences levied on the characters in the narrative. Games like “Papers Please” and “Beholder” levy this mechanic very well. In Orwell you cannot progress without giving the Antagonist certain information. This kills the illusion of choice, and make the rest of the narrative lose it's bite. Because I cannot NOT provide certain information the consequences are not my fault. The game made me do it. Especially in those moments where you have several data points you can give, and you need to choose between them, but if you choose wrong the game does not go forward, you end up throwing whatever data points at the wall, even those bits of data you do not want to provide, in order to get the game to continue. 

I realize why it was written this way. You cannot write a narrative which has ALL possibilities. So in order to move forward you need the player to trip certain triggers. An elegant way around this in my opinion would be to allow the information to be presented in "real time." This allows the narrative to continue while allowing the player more of a choice in the way it unfolds. I think this would greatly improve the impact of the game. 

The Twist - (mild spoiler warning) 
If you have read this far then I doubt this will really be a spoiler, but just in case, you have been warned.


There is a twist at the end. All good who-done-it's have them. This is no exception. My issue with the twist at the end of Orwell dove tails in to the idea of choice. There is no way you the player, let alone the character you play in the game, could predict it. There are no data points that I found that will allow you to discover the twist in game. Therefore it feels arbitrary. Once again the narrative loses impact because it does not feel like the player could intercede. The game is going to do what it is going to do and you are just pulled along to see what happens. that is what novels, TV shows, movies, and comic books are for. In fact I could see this story being a great Rashamon-Style comic, but as an interactive fiction I think this game falls flat. 

Summery - In summation I think if you are interested in games as an art form, or are just curios about what happens in this particular narrative, then this is worth while. I look forward to see if any of these issues are fixed in the next chapter. I do not regret my time "playing" this game. but I think in the end, The impact of the events was greatly blunted by the mechanics with which the narrative is presented. That seems a shame to me as the story could be quit impact-full if only the illusion of choice was maintained through out. In a narrative the promise of the premise is key, 
"Only the information you provide will be seen by the security forces and acted upon. You decide what gets seen and what does not, influencing how the suspects will be perceived." 
and this narrative missed that promise.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw: Orwell is basically just working but with more steps. Thankfully I got it on sale, but I wouldn’t recommend it as I felt I was just doing admin work the whole time. Osmotic Studios, a small German indie team, made this 2016 surveillance thriller where you play as a government agent using the Orwell system to dig through people’s emails, chats, social media, and documents after some incidents in a fictional country that feels a lot like a modern Western nation. You highlight and upload data, make choices about what goes into official reports, and watch the consequences play out. There’s a sequel too (Ignorance is Strength), which I've read is the same basic formula. Now the concept is clever on paper, digital Big Brother stuff inspired by the real world, and the writing tries to be thoughtful about privacy versus security.What I didn’t like: the actual gameplay is almost entirely reading walls of text, clicking highlighted bits, and filing them away. It starts feeling like busywork pretty fast, scrolling through inboxes, profiles, and logs for the next piece of info to stamp and upload. The interface is clean and the story has some twists, but the loop never evolves much beyond do your paperwork. It can drag, and the moral dilemmas lose punch when the moment-to-moment experience is so dry and repetitive. Not much in the way of challenge or variety either.If you must play it, stick to PC where it runs fine and the mouse and keyboard setup suits the desktop-sim style. Overall though, not for me. 4/10.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Creepy and well-written, Orwell tells the tale of what happens when the state gets unfettered access to your communication data, whether that be from the telephone or the internet. It's very topical, but it should be added that the scope of the access you have makes the recent "Snooper's Charter" in the UK look like lightweight. Nevertheless, your ability to screw with people's lives really hits home, especially when the twist at the end is revealed and all the consequences of your actions - and how misinterpreted data can be overblown - is laid bare.


That said, the game stays rather neutral in its moralising. It's clear the developers are anti-surveillance, as those *for* it would find the moral ambiguity of this game inconvenient, but they are not trying to whack you over the head with ideology. If you decide to come to the conclusion that, despite being messy at times, surveillance is a necessary evil then this game allows you to come to that conclusion. But it's going to push the extremes of what all-encompassing surveillance can do before it lets you come to that conclusion.

And while the politics of this game are clearly unavoidable, Orwell is also a pretty neat detective story, if not very typical. Instead of being in the front line looking for evidence, your sleuthing is invisible, but otherwise it has all the hallmarks of a good whodunnit, including red herrings, characters with strong motivations, and a twist at the end.

I'm not sure what else to say, really. It's pretty good and I happily recommend it.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell is engrossing and more than a bit disturbing considering the implications of some very real things that are happening in the world right now. More of an interactive novel than a proper game, it nonetheless pulled me in for the 3-4 hours it took to reach the end of it, as well as a couple of replays to try out different paths.

It's not perfect, though; there's no challenge in actually getting the information you require since it's highlighted for you and you simply have to upload it, which sort of takes most of the initiative out of your hands. You do get to decide how certain characters are viewed based on how much you pass on to the powers that be, and your choices affect how they're treated and what happens to them, but the prevailing narrative is more or less canned, on-rails, and you can't do very much to affect how it plays out other than within a narrow scope. Some of the decisions you make do have very profound consequences for the individuals concerned, and the first time through I did have a few things I deeply regretted because of what happened as a result.


The biggest downside is that the game is short and fairly linear; there are only so many branches/possibilties to explore, so once you've exhausted them, there's really not much replay value.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
ORWELL is a hybrid game somewhere between visual novel and point and click adventure. In the game, you are an investigator hired by the nation in testing out a new law which allows the government to spy on its citizens in order to find criminals. While this doesn’t sound too far off from where we are today, we can assume ordinary citizens aren’t having their wires tapped and all their online activity personally searched into. But that blurred line between what in this game is fiction and what is potential reality is where the game really shines, and pushes me to giving this game a general recommendation.
ORWELL starts off with investigating into a bomb that went off on a popular plaza and investigating a person of interest who was at the plaza. This is the only cutscene in the game and I really need to say that it shows how ugly the art style is. ORWELL has this odd polygonal art style that just doesn’t look right, and the game does nothing to utilize the style as well. Take a game like Wind Waker and the cell shading is important to the overall feel of the game, and the entire game would be very different if they had gone in a more realistic style. ORWELL does not earn that right to have an abstract art style, and it looks all the worse because of it. 
After the explosion, you begin digging into the meat of the game, which is going through people’s internet presence and phone calls and finding condemning information about them to fit them for the crime. The writing here then would be the important aspect to take away, and getting generally invested in the world or ORWELL should take precedence. However, this is another place where if the world of ORWELL was given to another developer with another vision, it probably would’ve been much more successful in world building that ORWELL currently is. The characters all generally fall into 2 categories; people who rebel against the government and people who are roped into rebelling against the government, and as such you get a lot of “it’s us or big brother vibes” when making your decisions which tends to not make the decisions feel organic. At several points in the game you can choose whether to report certain information to your supervisor and it affects how the supervisor views the target. However, these choices are often obviously superficial, and the contrasting information that you can give is usually contradicting in the sense that some information is outdated while other information is up to date. This is different than what an actual Orwellian inspired piece would aim for, where there are 2 facts that cannot exist within the same space and you are forced to accept both. For example, one contrasting information you need to choose between uploading to your supervisor is someone’s address. One is obviously right, and the other is outdated. It doesn’t mean the person didn’t use to previously live at the outdated address, but it’s just a matter of relevance. The game would be cooler if there were more instances of actual “doublethink” moments, instead of relying on portraying certain information in a correct or incorrect way. 
Speaking of being more Orwellian, the world of ORWELL is loaded with references to the novel by George Orwell, 1984. But this is another reason why the experience of the game is cheapened. A lot of the characters in the game are obvious references to people in 1984 and other dystopian media, such as a friend named Huxley or using the screenname w1n5t0n. If done sparingly, this could’ve been a neat little nod to the works of Orwell, but literally every character you interact with has some connection to the book, and the writing again suffers. It’s no longer a “hey, that’s a pretty neat reference,” but more so a “none of these characters seem original because the source material is being way overused.”
Ok, so all I’ve done is talk about the bad art style, the lacking writing, and non-significance of the gameplay, so why would I still recommend it? The reason I recommend it is because of that blurred line I mentioned at the beginning. That feel where you feel like you are gathering information about just another ordinary citizen, your mind begins to go what would this world really be like? If I send this review to my friends on messenger, what could someone get from my writing of it? One of the other things that happens a lot in the game is the people you talk to get implicated as well, so if I sent a message saying I was planning an attack to my group of friends, in ORWELL, everyone would be investigated on to find more evidence behind my potential crime and if they were involved in anyway. I think when some paths lead nowhere in ORWELL, it’s only a natural consequence that not everyone is going to be a criminal in the eyes of the government, but following the path to the end is pretty satisfying in the game. Despite the lackluster writing and world building, you do actually feel a voyeuristic guilt looking into everyone life between their social media accounts, medical records, college attendance, job records, blog posts, and so on. You can’t help but think if someone were to investigate me, they would find my screennames, my posts all over the internet, my video replays from streaming, and could trace words I said years ago to implicate me in something I was not a part of.
Altogether, the game has obvious flaws. It’s short, it has a forgettable art style, forgettable characters, and overall a forgettable plot. But playing through everything and seeing how everything plays out is thrilling in a way that no other game has ever provided for me. There is an ORWELL season 2 planned, and if they could just step away from the source material and feel more liberty to explore the world they’ve gone ahead and made, a lot of the issues I have with season 1 would be rectified. Overall, a 7/10. If you like dystopian media and the thought be being a voyeur into the lives of the ordinary citizens, give it a shot.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You is a thought-provoking narrative simulation developed by Osmotic Studios and published by Daedalic Entertainment that places the player in the uncomfortable role of a government surveillance operative. Rather than offering power fantasies or conventional heroism, the game asks you to sit behind a screen, analyze fragments of people’s digital lives, and decide which pieces of information deserve official attention. Set in the fictional state known simply as The Nation, the story unfolds in the aftermath of a violent terrorist attack, where fear, public pressure, and political urgency justify the rapid expansion of a system capable of monitoring nearly every aspect of a citizen’s existence.

The central mechanic revolves around the Orwell surveillance system itself, a sleek but unsettling interface through which you access emails, chat logs, social media profiles, news articles, phone records, and private files. Gameplay consists of identifying relevant “datachunks” and uploading them into official investigation dossiers. What makes this process compelling is that not all information is equally meaningful, nor is it always truthful when stripped of context. A casual message, a sarcastic comment, or an old association can become damning evidence once formalized inside the system. The act of choosing what to submit becomes the game’s primary decision-making tool, transforming seemingly mundane interactions into high-stakes moral choices.

Narratively, Orwell unfolds across multiple in-game days, each representing a new phase of the investigation and introducing fresh characters, revelations, and complications. The pacing is deliberate, allowing tension to build gradually as threads intertwine and suspects emerge. Rather than presenting clear villains and heroes, the story thrives on ambiguity. Individuals under scrutiny are complex, flawed, and often sympathetic, and the more you learn about them, the more uncomfortable the process of surveillance becomes. The game excels at showing how partial truths can snowball into irreversible consequences, especially when filtered through institutional authority.

A defining strength of Orwell is its ethical focus. The game consistently challenges the player to reflect on the power they wield and the ease with which that power can be misused. Uploading information feels procedural and routine, yet the consequences are often deeply personal for the people affected. Careers are ruined, relationships collapse, and lives spiral based on decisions made in silence behind a terminal. The game does not present clear “right” answers; instead, it forces players to confront the reality that surveillance systems are shaped as much by human judgment and bias as by data itself.

Visually, Orwell adopts a minimalist, utilitarian aesthetic that reinforces its themes. Interfaces resemble real-world operating systems and investigative software, grounding the experience in plausibility rather than spectacle. This stripped-down presentation keeps attention focused on text, decisions, and implications rather than visual distraction. Sound design is similarly restrained, using subtle cues rather than dramatic music to maintain an atmosphere of quiet tension and bureaucratic detachment. The result is an experience that feels unsettling precisely because of how ordinary and believable it is.

Player agency is a key component of the experience, though it is intentionally constrained. While the overarching investigation follows a structured path, the specific outcomes depend heavily on what information you choose to reveal or withhold. Multiple endings and branching consequences encourage replayability, as players can explore how different ethical approaches alter the narrative. Some may approach the game as a dutiful analyst focused solely on public safety, while others may attempt to protect individual privacy whenever possible. Each approach reveals different facets of the story and reinforces the game’s central question: who decides what is justified when security and freedom collide?

Reception to Orwell has been consistently positive, particularly among players who value narrative depth and social commentary. Many praise its relevance, especially in an era defined by data collection, algorithmic profiling, and online identity. While some may find the gameplay slow or limited due to its text-heavy nature, those willing to engage with its pacing often find it deeply immersive and emotionally resonant. The lack of traditional action is not a weakness but a deliberate design choice that underscores the quiet, insidious nature of surveillance.

Ultimately, Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You stands as a powerful example of how games can explore modern societal issues with nuance and restraint. It transforms data analysis into a dramatic and morally charged experience, reminding players that information is never neutral and that those who control it shape reality itself. For players interested in narrative-driven games that challenge assumptions and provoke reflection rather than offer escapism, Orwell delivers a memorable and unsettling journey that lingers long after the screen goes dark.

review_text_raw:
A poignant game on the times we live in. I'm a humongous fan of the "Walking Simulator" genre and I stumbled upon this game during the Steam Winter Sale (3 days ago). Orwell has a captivating storyline that takes the "first person" experience quite literally. Without spoiling the game, the story focuses on a user operated software called Orwell, where the player assumes the role as a operator outside the fictatious "Nation", spying on activists that are tagged as potentially violent. 

The user interface is streamlined, dare I say "user-friendly". The fictional profiles depicted in the video game are unnervingly real, pulling me into the experience, as though as I really am spying on others. The characters are well scripted, albeit being scripts of text. The characters are caricatures of stereotypical activists, with complex backgrounds and hidden agendas. 

The "orwellian" connotations that are hinted at in the game are subtle, nuanced without being too overbearing or obvious. As you progressively submit information on labelled targets, you start to feel a heavy burden of responsibility on your shoulders. The multiple options and consequences from submitting false information add more weight to the situation. The activities or rituals performed by the main character are a frighteningly realistic, depecting the state of the world we live in. 

My only complaints include the duration of the game: it is rather short in length, more like a concept game showcasing some of the developer's strengths. The waiting times between each mission is abysmal, sometimes resulting in multiple crashes. 

All in all, this is an underrated gem in the walking simulator category, standing tall with the likes of Gone Home and Soma.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
What a wasted opportunity.

I went into this game wanting to like it - I really did. To be clear - I played through the entire game, finishing each of the 5 chapters.

Orwell is ostensibly a game about a surveillance state gone terribly wrong - but almost at every opportunity, it fails to make any meaningful point and constantly gets in its own way.

It starts bad. Rather than giving you, as a player, the agency to incriminate and potentially ruin the lives of the people you are surveilling, the game immediately puts you at arms-length. You are nothing more than a data collector with the ability to find and store information, but not make any meaningful analysis or conclusions about this data. Worse, it pairs you with the clumsily-written and drearily heavy-handed Symes - the *actual* investigator, who acts on the information you upload and is a constant source of awkward, immersion-breaking, and stupid commentary. 

It's true that, in principle, the data you choose to upload can affect the lives and outcomes of the people whose privacy you're invading - the trouble is that there's no real incentive to do so. Oftentimes, you must upload certain pieces of data in order to move the story along - which makes sense, because you're nothing more than a glorified data monkey clicking blue text and throwing it into a database. If you choose to hide a piece of information, it's not clear whether or not you'll be able to progress through the story. If you get something wrong (in the extremely limited range of things you are even allowed to get wrong), there are few consequences - an issue exacerbated by how distanced you are from everything that goes down. You don't really get to make the call, figure out the deduction, or even choose whether or not you should be wielding the awesome power you do. You either progress the story, or you don't - Symes is the one who gets to actually decide.

What's worse is that each of the characters in the game are utterly unlikable - the crimes you investigate them for are legitimate crimes that hurt real innocents and pose genuine dangers to the society in which they inhabit - the moral quandary that this game should so naturally lend itself to (the invasion of privacy, the loss of intimacy, that everybody is a criminal under mass surveillance, etc.,) is utterly and absolutely wasted. Instead, you are railroaded through a specific set of documents, webpages, and chats (not giving you any opportunity to actually deduce anything) in which not one of the horribly written characters manages to endear themselves.

Ultimately, this game is trying to tell you two stories - a by the numbers B-grade mystery plot filled with unlikable and annoying characters, and a study of the evolution of mass surveillance in an increasingly tech-focussed society. In so doing, they tell neither one well. They did an incredible disservice to a barely-interesting character study of modern revolutionaries, and an even greater disservice to the core (and seemingly obvious!) issues with state-driven, indiscriminate surveillance.

Let's not even start with the UI. What begins as a somewhat interesting ability to listen in on conversations quickly becomes a tiresome and arduous chore - there are a couple of moments in which listening in on a conversation live makes sense, but these moments are few and far between. For the most part, you are treated to a disastrously slow chat message filled with stilted dialogue and unfortunate Fellow Kids idioms, or an equally slow voice transcription. I quickly began to dread these moments, rather than feel the rush of uncovering a potential clue.

At no point do you feel like a data wizard, an unscrupulous detective, or even a curious and detached researcher. You just feel bored. 

Orwell is, despite its polished presentation, a total and undeniable bust. 

Desperately trying to cram all of the social commentary it should have been exploring over the entire game into its final chapter, it fails to make a meaningful statement about mass surveillance and the police state. 

Having written shallow, stupid, stereotypical characters with zero likable traits or humanizing aspects (each of whom are also genuine suspects in an act of actual terrorism) it fails to present a compelling character study of the 21st-century revolutionary.

By railroading you during every part of the core gameplay loop and anchoring you at the waist with a bumbling, intrusive character (who gets to make *all* the calls and draw all the *actual* conclusions), they fail to provide a satisfying, thrilling, or even baseline interesting detective experience.

Finally, by forgetting the most fundamental principles in their clunky, limited, and careless design, they failed to provide an even halfway tolerable interface. 

I didn't even get to enjoy interacting with the game.

Orwell is a disaster. You will get nothing from it, no insight, no emotion, no deductions, and no surprises. It wastes every bit of the opportunity it had to say something meaningful.

This is my Two Minutes Hate - and Orwell deserves every second of it.

Instead, you are railroaded through a specific set of documents, webpages, and chats (not giving you any opportunity to actually deduce anything) in which not one of the horribly written characters manages to endear themselves. Ultimately, this game is trying to tell you two stories - a by the numbers B-grade mystery plot filled with unlikable and annoying characters, and a study of the evolution of mass surveillance in an increasingly tech-focussed society. In so doing, they tell neither one well. They did an incredible disservice to a barely-interesting character study of modern revolutionaries, and an even greater disservice to the core (and seemingly obvious!) issues with state-driven, indiscriminate surveillance. Let's not even start with the UI. What begins as a somewhat interesting ability to listen in on conversations quickly becomes a tiresome and arduous chore - there are a couple of moments in which listening in on a conversation live makes sense, but these moments are few and far between. For the most part, you are treated to a disastrously slow chat message filled with stilted dialogue and unfortunate Fellow Kids idioms, or an equally slow voice transcription. I quickly began to dread these moments, rather than feel the rush of uncovering a potential clue. At no point do you feel like a data wizard, an unscrupulous detective, or even a curious and detached researcher. You just feel bored. Orwell is, despite its polished presentation, a total and undeniable bust. Desperately trying to cram all of the social commentary it should have been exploring over the entire game into its final chapter, it fails to make a meaningful statement about mass surveillance and the police state. Having written shallow, stupid, stereotypical characters with zero likable traits or humanizing aspects (each of whom are also genuine suspects in an act of actual terrorism) it fails to present a compelling character study of the 21st-century revolutionary. By railroading you during every part of the core gameplay loop and anchoring you at the waist with a bumbling, intrusive character (who gets to make *all* the calls and draw all the *actual* conclusions), they fail to provide a satisfying, thrilling, or even baseline interesting detective experience. Finally, by forgetting the most fundamental principles in their clunky, limited, and careless design, they failed to provide an even halfway tolerable interface. I didn't even get to enjoy interacting with the game. Orwell is a disaster. You will get nothing from it, no insight, no emotion, no deductions, and no surprises. It wastes every bit of the opportunity it had to say something meaningful. This is my Two Minutes Hate - and Orwell deserves every second of it.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1] How far are you willing to go to protect the populace? [/h1]

[i]Orwell[/i] is a “visual novel” style game in which you have the ability to follow cyber-breadcrumbs in order to slowly uncover suspect’s online lives. Your goal? Stop a terrorist organization (?) from bombing public spaces. Your tools? As an agent, you are privy to the entirety of your target’s posts, articles, phone calls, emails, etc. Use this information to reveal more and more relevant webpages and conversations. The catch? You’re overlooked by a supervisor and you must choose what information to upload. This supervisor can only see the bits of information you feed him, so choose wisely or risk ruining an innocent’s life. The challenge? Upload only enough information to gain new leads, but not jump to conclusions. 

Are you really helping the greater good by invading the privacy of the few? Or have you caused more harm than good, muddling in affairs you should have never been in? Are the internet spies of today, really the superheroes of tomorrow? Find out by stepping into these large, cyber shoes. Act quickly and stop a harmful event in its tracks, or wait it out and discover it was a false alarm. Big brother is watching you. You are watching the people. Lives are on the line. Decide. 

Then watch as you say, [b]“I never meant for this to happen.”[/b]

Let me start off this review by saying I’m one who really enjoys a story-based game. I particularly enjoy consequence based story games (like [i]Telltale[/i]). If that’s not your cup of tea, this game is not for you. If you’re still interested, here’s the pros and cons for the game so far.

[h1]Pros:[/h1] [b]Interesting social commentary.[/b] There’s no denying that this is the age of technology, and with that comes a whole new slew of problems that our forefathers never could have foresaw when drafting the constitution. [i]Orwell[/i] heavily and obviously alludes to the current hot topics of freedom of internet access, government access to our personal files and correspondences, and general cyber security we see crop up in the news time and time again. 

[b]Easy interface.[/b] There’s not much to learn but drag and drop. Your un-uploaded data chunks are marked so you don’t lose track of what you’ve read, need to read, and are saving for later.

[b]More unique game flow.[/b] Events don’t happen unless you upload data chucks, leaving you to explore the branches of plot in whatever order feels natural to you. It does still feel a bit restricted, though, (see “A bit linear, limited” in cons) a perhaps more of a pseudo-free-directional choice. (But isn’t the concept of freedom what this game is all about?) 

[b]Intriguing artwork.[/b] The geometric artistic style lends itself to unconsciously nod its head towards the cyber-oriented world of the game. It ties in beautifully to the theme of the game—from the logo to the interface—without being too aggressive.

[h1]Cons:[/h1] [strike][b]A better save system!![/b][/strike] Update has added a rewind system, but I have not played since [strike]I cannot stress this enough. Since this is a consequence-based game, I’d like to be able to start from the end episode one, or so, with my decisions staying the same, and only make changes to my decisions from there out, with my profiles branching out from my first play through plot line. Starting over from the beginning is too much of a grind. Even a way to speed up messaging/call text on the second (and beyond) playthrough would be better for acheivement hunters or people just curious about the other endings. Examples of games with a good save system for this style of gameplay include [i]A Wolf Among Us[/i] and [i]Papers, Please.[/i][/strike]

[b]A bit linear, limited.[/b] There were some moments I wish some bit of text was highlighted (you may only drag and upload highlighted data chunks) since I wanted to explore that avenue of inquiry, but [i]Orwell[/i] had other plans. This gave the game a restricted feeling. It does not leave the game open to a world of naturally-occurring red herrings (only game-constructed ones, not user constructed), which I think would have added much more depth to the game. Also, it’s glaringly obvious which pieces of text carry great significance. (Those will be the ones with conflicting evidence) so sometimes the challenge of deciding to report information right away or wait was quite discernible, offering no challenge. Although, I will say that there are a few nuggets of data I uploaded without believing they would have as large of a consequence as they did. 

[b]Short.[/b] There’s only a little over forty minutes of game play per episode, and with five episodes, this leads to roughly four hours of gameplay (assuming you don’t replay events). I follow a rule of thumb of at least $1 to 1 hour of gameplay, so in that regard, it’s a bit pricey. Just wait for a sale. 

[h1]Remark:[/h1] [b]Play in one sitting[/b] (or as close to that as possible, if you don't have a full 4-5 hours to dedicate to one game) The flow and length of the game lends itself to be optimally played in one sitting. Taking a break and not have a comprehensive refresher (like the cinematic playbacks of key choices in [i]Telltale[/i] games) of your choices and actions is jarring to the enjoyment of the storyline in my opinion.

[h1]Conclusion:[/h1]
[b]I’d recommend buying [i]Orwell[/i] when on sale.[/b] It has an interesting and captivating storyline, despite some need of polishing. The interface, flow, and artwork lend itself to be an immersive experience into the lives of the people you are spying on to protect. Also, the current social commentary gives a real-world depth to the game. It does feel a bit restricting at times, and the story is short. The save system leaves much to be desired, since I would like to more easily explore all possibilities of my choices. But, despite these factors it was still enjoyable and fun to play.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I have been playing video games since the Atari 2600 and out of the many games I have played only 5  have inspired me to award them my own personal score of 10. Orwell has joined this very exclusive list for me. The game is a masterclass of using the medium of video games to make poignant social commentary that feels gripping and authentic. 

Daniel Marx (Game Designer) is a fantastic writer who gives each one of his characters a very distinct voice using colloquial dialogue and expressions that stay consistent for each character throughout the course of the 5 chapters of the story. His ability to create believable characters with personalities and motivations that feel real is the key to making the message of the game resonate. This isn't a simple story of noble heroes and evil villains, this is an examination of complex people and their struggles to reconcile their beliefs and their feelings, their fears and their ability to summon up the courage to do what they feel is right. 

The Gameplay is simple to understand, but choices made by the player do have branching consequences. Reminiscent of Telltale games and other members of the narrrative genre with a choice driven structure. The game manages to give the player a sense of real agency in the outcomes of the story, and have genuinley significant differences at several key moments. My mind spins at the challenge of writing a story that is able to stay consistent throughout its length, and yet offer a significant number of alternatives that need to be followed to their logical conclusion. Again, my compliments to Daniel Marx on his writing skills and game design. Impressive. Very impressive. 

The art style reminded me of the polygonal look of games like Out of This World and Flashback from the early and mid 90's with improved technology that looks good and yet remains accessible to all players even ones with 8 year old laptops (such as myself). Compliments to Melanie Taylor for an aesthetic that is easy on the eye and hardware. 

In the end, the writing, gameplay and art all serve to execute on making a statement about the ever increasing surveillance that is taking place in our own world and it is no suprise that the invasion of privacy that is possible at this very moment is something that can chill to the bone. We are at a crossroads in the story of humanity, whether the next chapters are dominated by the decision to sacrifice freedom for security or the acceptance that freedom carries risks, but is far better than a world where everyone is always suspect of being an enemy of the state and a target for elimination. 

Provided you do not object to reading a great deal (as there is no voice acting), this game will provide you with 10 hours of riveting narrative that will undoubtedly leave you questioning how much autonomy we are willing to surrender for the illusion of safety that a large surveillance state seemingly affords. 

I cannot recommend this game highly enough.

P.S. Additionally many thanks to Michael Kluge (Programming) for his coding work. The game runs very well. Amazing that this trio of developers crafted such a landmark title. I bow to your triumvirate of talent. 

P.P.S : Incidentally, in case anyone is interested, my other Perfect 10 games are :

- Legend of Zelda : Ocarina of Time
- Resident Evil 4
- Batman : Arkham City
- Last of Us
- Telltale's The Walking Dead : Season 1

Very different from Orwell, but masterpieces for me in the revolution in video game design they brought to different elements of the industry.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell is a game that I have mixed feeling about. While I did enjoy the game, I also want to clarify that there is certainly more than one issue with the game that makes me want to not recommend it.

The gameplay boils down to one and only one mechanic. Being able to drag selected text into a profile which affects the story. You need to bounce between internet pages, phone-call logs, and a few other forms of data to find keywords and important text to upload. Depending on what you upload, what the government believes and what happens to the person(s) involved changes. Do you portray a spoiled brat as a terrorist? An old man as a kind teacher. You decide what information they've put online defines them, very literally. 

The issues I have with this is as such: 
[olist]
    [*]Choices don't ultimately matter.
    [*]It is painfully short.
    [*]A lack of any audio design.
[/olist]

From top to bottom, the linearity of the game. Despite being able to chose what information does or doesn't get uploaded, a lot (and I do mean a LOT) of events will happen regardless of your actions. The game literally says in it's description: "But, be warned, the information you supply will have consequences." However, despite this, the only things my choices ended up affecting were the achievements. And spoiler alert: [spoiler] You can get any of the three endings no matter what choices you made in previous episodes. [/spoiler] Sure, on a superficial surface level your choices have consequences, but these "consequences" never actually impact your story or gameplay expericence.

Onto the next, the length. You may see me having 7.5 hours and tell me "Oh well 7.5 hours in NOT a short game!" You'd be right. Except Orwell is not 7.5 hours long, it is 3 hours long at most and 2 hours long at it's shortest. The only reason I have more than 3 hours of playtime is because I went back to get all of the achievements, which is also why i know how little your choices affect the story. I've seen all the endings, seen the affect of almost all of the choices, and even then with some time spent idle I was able to see 99% of this game's offerings in under 8 hours. This isn't inherently bad, but Orwell has little to no gameplay, audio design, or anything. It's just an on rails story, and for it to be that short for a $10 USD price tag is a little much.

Lastly, the audio design. As previously mentioned, there is little to no audio in this game. You have 3 music tracks, the main menu theme, the basic ambient theme and a more intense theme for when things "get serious." Outside of the music, you might have a few computer beeps or a quick musical tone at random points, but they're so spread out that a majority of your time is spent with almost nothing going into your ears. You can't hear people on their phone calls, your boss can't speak to you, there are no audio transcripts. It is the most barebones audio design I've seen in a story driven game.

The only really good thing I'd argue in favor of is the art style. It is a fractal/cubism artstyle that absolutely draws you in. The issue is that this art style is not the primary focus, instead that focus is on a painfully bland UI. game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I'll be honest, this one surprised me! And I actually had decent expectations to begin with. After playing the demo I figured it'd be a well done pick-your-own-adventure sort of deal, dressed up as something more intricate, but I'd say this went well beyond that. Simply put, the demo really is just a taste of what comes later. The game does a lot with the limited gameplay it has available. The story handles the subject matter fantastically and actually managed to surprise me (and it's quite a relevant tale these days). The final chapter was genuinely tense and left me constantly reconsidering my options. I'd have to play it again to see how much of the choices were an illusion, but it did feel like actions genuinely had large and unforeseen consequences. 

I have some small complaints, like I sometimes felt that I should be able to override the conflicting data chunks or felt stuck while the game waited for me to upload chunks for which I didn't feel I had enough justification to upload them, but some of that is part of the story and some of it is just the limitations of a narrative like this. Overall, they're fairly minor issues.

I can wholeheartedly recommend the game at full price and I'm looking forward to the sequel.

If you like puzzle, mystery and crime solving games, then this game is for you!
"But what is different with this game when compared to other games in the same genre?"
Well, Orwell puts you in a human researcher's perspective. As a researcher you have the power to spy on suspects freely, and choose what info should appear in their profile, even if unnecessary.
Be careful, however, because people WILL die if you make the wrong choices (but hey, at least you get achievements for this). Everything has consequences.
The gameplay is simple and you can get into this game easily (if you know how to read).
The story is thrilling and entertaining. The tension when you see a new article after you've done a wrong choice is great.
I recommend this game to anyone that is a fan of these genres, or for people that have never played a game like this and want to get into this.
