game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell is an investigative game akin to a visual novel. You play as The Investigator, someone whose job it is to use the powerful Orwell surveillance system to solve crimes – or in this case, solve a particular crime. You see, a bomb was set off in Freedom Plaza in The Nation, killing three people, and it is your job to try and catch the bomber before they can kill anyone else.

Orwell is more like an interactive novel than an ordinary video game – the game is wholly centered around reading text for about four and a half hours, and while it has more meaningful interaction than most visual novels, the actual gameplay itself is very simple and not very action-oriented. It is a very cerebral experience, and if reading lots of text isn’t your cup of tea, this is not the game for you.

You start out with a single person of interest – a young woman who left the Plaza shortly before the bomb went off. She was a protester who had been arrested for attacking a police officer, but who wasn’t prosecuted for it due to lack of evidence. It quickly becomes clear that not all is as it seems, and it seems unlikely that she personally was the bomber – but she has past associations with a group known as Thought, an anti-government group which often engages in extremist rhetoric. But are they really the sort of people who would kill people? Or are they just innocent bystanders coincidentally caught up in the investigation?

Orwell is a very ambiguous game, and it is precisely this ambiguity which really makes the game work. Thought is upset about living in a surveillance state, but it is clear from your perspective as The Investigator that the system is designed to be humane in many ways – the investigator passes on information to someone else, whose job it is to analyze the data. You cannot investigate people who aren’t targets – unless someone has been designated as suspicious by actual data, you cannot collect data at all them, nor are you allowed to go snooping through their things. But if they are a target of interest, you have nigh unlimited authority to go snooping. And while the state is clearly a bit authoritarian, it is also clear that the system works – crime has gone down, and you can catch several criminals over the course of the game who really did do bad things. The person on the other end, who helps to determine whether or not the data is really indicative of wrongdoing, is a genuinely nice person who cares about people and who urges you to collect more data. The leader of The Nation appears to genuinely be trying to help out neighboring states.

But all of this is muddied with the ambiguity of the fact that not everyone in the government is nice, and the general sinister nature of your surveillance. Your actions do have consequences, and it is clear that if you made the wrong decisions, you could potentially feed people bad data and get people put in jail – and the choice of whether or not to feed people bad data, and the impression you leave the government on people, is dependent on what data you give them.

The game, thus, is a combination of an investigation and a moral choice system – you are not only investigating who might be the bomber, but also deciding what is and is not relevant, what should and should not be part of the investigation, and you have the power to wrongfully put people in jail or put people in danger. The very simple gameplay of choosing what pieces of highlighted information to put into a database from various documents, webpages, emails, and phone and text conversations thus takes on a great deal of weight, and makes you think about what you’re doing in a very different way from other investigatory games, as you think of it not only in terms of true/false, but also whether the information morally belongs in the hands of the government.

The game’s gameplay also shows how a system like that can lead to paranoia, as you see people engage in a lot of extremist rhetoric and it is easy to jump to conclusions and morally convict someone in your mind who didn’t do anything worse than complain, as well as how easy it is to prejudge someone in the opposite direction as well, making you think more positively of them than they truly deserve. And it puts stress on the player as well – you cannot take back your actions, so if you incorrectly present someone as a dangerous criminal, you can’t fix it and have to live with the consequences.

How humane the system is – and who is in the right and wrong – is a complicated question that the game ultimately doesn’t answer for itself, but which the player answers via their actions throughout the game. Like “The Lady or the Tiger”, the way the player responds to the story really reflects as much on the player’s own evaluation of humanity, and how they weigh the risks and benefits of a system like that. Rather than being preachy about how evil the system is, the game also shows why people might like a system like that and want it to be implemented. It is perhaps the most even-handed presentation of the subject matter I’ve seen, and it achieves this by putting the player in the seat of someone who might be a part of such a system and showing just how ambiguous the system can be and how much power they wield, both how dangerous it can be if misused but how beneficial it can be if used appropriately.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1]A must-play for any cyber-security enthusiast[/h1]

[i]Received this as a gift from a dear friend[/i]

[b]Note:[/b]

Playing this game involves a lot of reading and if that's not your thing, you're probably not gonna enjoy Orwell.
But if you like playing VN's, I believe you'll love it!

[b]Gameplay:[/b]

You're an investigator in a secret mass-surveillance program run by the government, called Orwell (named after [url=https://youtu.be/h9JIKngJnCU]George Orwell, author of the novel '1984'[/url]).
Your job is to read up the information in your [i]Reader[/i] and upload [i]chunks[/i] of it to the Orwell database.
Uploading certain information may open up more leads and you may get unrestricted access to the 'target' person's PC, mobile, medical records and what not.

At certain times, you may find conflicting bits of information.
At such times, it's best to avoid resolving the issue. Read other relevant details and when you come back, it'd be clear to you what the right information is.

During the entire course of the game, all you do is read - a person's social network feed, their blogs. Sometimes you tap their calls and messages. But, you never directly interact with the individuals.
Yet, you gain so much knowledge about them that you practically know the person. Without actually [i]knowing[/i] them.
And all that just in the timeframe of 5 days!
It's kinda amazing and disturbing at the same time.

Also, the most important thing. Once an information is uploaded to Orwell, it cannot be deleted.
And there could be consequences depending on what you upload.
So, you wanna be careful, to not wrongly accuse an innocent. Which, trust me, is not that easy.

[b]My thoughts:[/b]
[i](May contain SPOILERS. Or it may simply affect your experience of the game. So read at your own risk ¯\_(ツ)_/¯ )[/i]

I loved the game.
Government mass surveillance has been a topic of concern for quite some time now.
It was ingenious to make a game that puts the player on the opposite side of the coin where the player is the one carrying out the surveillance.

At first, while it's all new and sunny, you feel like an unrivaled God - passing righteous judgments, punishing the wrong-doers. That is what you're made to believe you are.
And you find all sorts of crazy, unstable people in the world that you feel they [i]need[/i] to be surveilled.
Then you find out that they had a disturbing past that made them into what they are.
Then you realize that passing righteous judgments is a lot more difficult than you had initially assumed. And that personal data is a sensitive thing and it can destroy lives. And that YOU might be destroying someone's life as a part of your [i]work[/i].
If you're lucky, you'll wake up in time and realize how faulty the system is. And how you've been probing into other's personal lives and just how despicable that really is.
Otherwise, you either lose your humanity forever and become a Dementor that feeds on other people's personal lives. Or you go insane. Or both.

Maybe this journey of realization is similar to the one Edward Snowden had. Only, his journey was real and his actions had real consequences.
I would strongly recommend anyone to watch [url=http://www.imdb.com/title/tt3774114/]Snowden[/url] and [url=http://www.imdb.com/title/tt4044364/]Citizenfour[/url] after playing the game if you haven't already.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1]TL:DR[/h1]

If you expect the real CONSEQUENCES of YOUR actions - do not buy this game.
If you're ok with a tell-tale game with mostly textual narrative and poor amount of player choices - it's actually a good one and you really should try it. I only gave it thumb down because I'm personally not okay with the whole thing.

[h1]Now, the long review[/h1]

At first glance the game looks like a game about consequences. And it really tries to look like one. But in fact, it’s not. In the description they say "the information you supply will have consequences", but most of the game scriptwriters just lead you by the hand. It’s like playing a visual novel with dialogue options, but most of them have only one option (ridiculous, right?). Or two, both leading to the same branch but having different lines as reactions to them.
You see a chunk of info that will certainly make Symes do the wrong thing, because it's out of context, so you decide to omit it. BUT for the further story development it either won't affect a thing, or will be required for the script to go on.
You see the connection between two personages, it’s drawn at the relationships net after you add the corresponding datachunk. But you cannot fill the profile of that new guy, until he’s not a “target”, even tho you have tonns of info right before your eyes. Given there’s often no police records on the suspects, sometimes you’d really have done better with just google, no orwell system needed. So basically in Orwell you just search for the highlighted text in docs or chats and click on it.
And since there were no crucial info in all the unhighlighted text walls (and even if there were, you couldn't do anything about it if it's not highlighted as a data chunk) I've just begun to skip most of the text. The datachunks you see will lead you to the goal, and if there's a script branch, you won't miss it in most cases. But, again, it's hard to tell whether there's a branch (even for the "conflicting chunks") since there's like one real branch per day, and everything else doesn't really affect the day's outcome and seem to differ only in Symes' comments (and sometimes you can even notice mismatches in chains of his comments if you do something not in the order devs predicted ([spoiler]On the third day that Symes guy says "WOW, Harrison and Juliet were together! How interesting", while it's only UPDATE on the notion you make during the second day, Again, from 2nd day's start you get that they were together, but only at the end of the day you finally have a chance to add this to their files, therefore Symes only knows it at the end of the day, because he's out of context, which is FUKKEN STUPID AT THE FIRST PLACE[/spoiler]). 

The story is cool though. If we omit the poor gameplay and irrational investigator-symes thing, the story itself is really thrilling. I don’t think I’d last till the end of the first episode f it wasn’t for the story. 
 
But the story is not enough to recommend this piece of art as a game. Its gameplay and theme seem to be about choices, but in fact it’s just a point-and-click with prescripted everything.
Yet it’d be a great BOOK, if the player and Symes were united into single main character. Or it could be a good game with more VN-like gameplay (and again, division into invest and Symes-thing is YET WOULD BE ridiculous). But when you have a whole spy system at your control, you expect much more freedom.
Or, perhaps, that’s exactly the point - there’s no freedom in this game?

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h3][i]“War is peace. Freedom is slavery. Ignorance is strength.” [/i]- George Orwell[/h3]


Even if you haven't read anything by George Orwell, you've probably heard about 1984. The dystopia the author foresaw has undoubtedly materialized in the modern world, as most readers of the book like to point out. This assertion is without doubt true; even if you only use the internet for personal purposes, there are still a lot of data crumbs left behind. You can never be certain if someone is keeping an eye on your every online move, whether it be a post about a recent vacation, a comment made on a forum, or the address you use to sign emails. 
This is precisely what Orwell: Keeping an Eye on You promises: it is a game about a reality that nobody wants to face but that hangs in the air.

[h3][i]“The consequences of every act are included in the act itself.”[/i] - George Orwell[/h3]

The game takes place in the capital of a fictional country called The Nation, where on April 12th, 2017, a terrorist attack occurs: a bomb detonates in the famous Freedom Plaza, destroying a statue and killing several people. At the same time, the police receive a note containing the first three stanzas of a German folk song called The Thoughts are Free.

In 2012, The Party, a paternalistic government that leads The Nation, passed the Safety Bill, which gave the government complete freedom over citizens' personal data and the ability to spy on them using a surveillance system called Orwell. This is where your involvement with The Nation begins.
You are the first person who has been selected to be an investigator - a citizen outside of The Nation, who will use Orwell to uncover as much data about a person as possible. You are being accompanied by an Advisor, who will connect you to the authorities. 

The plot is essentially a classic detective whodunit story told in five chapters; throughout the game, multiple suspects will emerge, and your job will be to determine each person's involvement and, in the end, find the perpetrator(s) - or is it?
The aforementioned data (which the game refers to as datachucks) gathering is the game's main essence and gameplay mechanic - you have access to a wide range of websites, phones, e-mail addresses, and even computers, where you must find information related to your lead. This isn't a difficult task because the game highlights them in blue or yellow; the latter indicates a data collision, and you must determine which is the correct data.

A few things should be kept in mind with this mechanic: first, it is completely irreversible - once you upload something in the system, there is no way to change it, and the story will proceed accordingly; second, you do not need to upload every possible datachunk - at first, the game forces you to do this, but later you must be careful what you upload; and third, the game is actually a choose-your-own-adventure with a detective façade - given that there are multiple endings, your choices will have a heavy impact on the story.

Orwell's strength is the moral uncertainty it contains. Players will have to weigh the pros and cons of sharing new information with the people they're investigating versus keeping it to themselves as they gather additional evidence. Because of this, players will feel more invested in the game and more emotionally connected to their choices.

[h3][i]“But if thought corrupts language, language can also corrupt thought.” [/i]- George Orwell[/h3]

One of the game's greatest strengths is its immersive and atmospheric presentation. The dark and minimalist art style, combined with a haunting original soundtrack, sets the perfect tone for an oppressive world governed by The Party. The user interface is sleek and intuitive, allowing easy navigation of the vast amount of information at your disposal. Towards the end of the game, the interface will get much more crowded; however, the game displays a red icon next to a document where new data chunks can be found. Furthermore, the game's soundtrack perfectly complements the dystopian atmosphere, with haunting melodies and industrial beats that immerse players in the world of surveillance and control. 

Orwell does, however, have a few minor flaws. As the investigation progresses through a series of data-mining tasks, the gameplay can feel slow at times. Some players, particularly those who prefer more action-oriented experiences, may find these moments tedious. Furthermore, while the game encourages players to take different paths, the overall impact of your choices on the narrative can feel somewhat limited, leaving some room for a more dynamic and personalized experience unexplored.
The length of the game is another aspect of the experience that could be improved. The story is interesting and the decisions are weighty, yet the game is over in a matter of hours and it left me craving for more. The game's depth of topic and potential for replay may have benefited from more content or branching routes.



[h3][i]“Freedom is the freedom to say that two plus two make four. If that is granted, all else follows.”[/i]
 - George Orwell[/h3]

Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You is a fascinating and unsettling adventure that delves into the moral issues raised by omniscient monitoring and the misuse of authority. A standout in the narrative-driven genre, thanks to its engaging tale, accessible gameplay, and morally weighty choices. Even though it's not particularly long and has a few weaker points, it's a must-play if you enjoy engaging stories set in dystopian futures.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I wish I could give this a rating... Like "B+" or "70%".     

I came here having tried Orwell a few years ago and didn't take to it... Then I played "Return of the Obra Dinn" and was so entranced by it I searched for "Game like..." and this came up, so I went back and started over.

I'll just say that this game is NOTHING like "Return of the Obra Dinn".    It feels like the "Walking Simulator" of detective games. You don't 'detect' so to speak, more than you just walk through scads and scads of documents and photographs, and picking out important pieces that are pre-highlighted for you.  Occasionally you get to make a moral / ambiguous choice between two things with far too little / ambiguous information.   This is kind of the point of the game... To show how easily we can be led down a path of conclusion based on scant evidence... Is the player 'aware' enough of the situation to select the correct interpretation.  Sometimes it's easy, sometimes it's not.

Where Orwell falls down is that the consequence of what you pull out of the documentation isn't always clear.   You can be pulling out loads of stuff, with the occasional snide / snippy remark from your 'advisor', with no noticeable progress in the game.  Then all of a sudden, you pick something and *BOOM*  the whole world spins on its axis, and you suddenly get more context, albeit too late.

Now, as I said, the 'late information binding' thang is the whole Orwell shtick, but it's really s****g annoying when you're playing.  It's only in the end game, that the whole POINT of the game becomes clear and you realise that the annoyance you're feeling has a purpose.

Then the game offers you a moral choice...   Carry on, or rebel.  For me, the decision was pretty clear cut, but it didn't look like it had much effect, tbh.     And that's the other big issue, is that you're never sure if you chose correctly, wrongly, or your choice made no major difference.  Some might say this adds 'replayability', but to be honest, I don't think I can be bothered clicking through dozens of semi-meaningless PDFs for another 10 hours to choose different outcomes to test the theory....


I kinda enjoyed playing Orwell... But there were times when I just wanted the story to advance, but it simply refused because I had to make a choice.   And by this point, there was so little context, and so much cruft to wade through, I gave up and just picked one option to make the game carry on.   Perhaps that was the point as well.. I dunno. It's midnight and my brain hurts from reading all this text on the screen.

It's under a tenner on Steam right now. I can't remember how I got Orwell, but if I paid over £10, I don't think I got a good price/enjoyment ratio.    It's a relatively solid game, and has a fair point to make on the way the surveillance state is going, and had great music, good visuals and an interesting setting.  Get it if you like making your own deductions and choices.

review_text_raw:
I bought Orwell (on sale) expecting a sort of 1984 screens, eyes, with wiretaps everywhere. What I got was a message pop up game with a pretty compelling story. In that sentence, I just described the whole review. If you didn't get it - keep reading!

They say it's wrong to assume, and definitely after playing this, it's wrong to make assumptions sometimes. If there is a demo available, try it! This one didn't have it, and it was on sale - so I went for it. The [b]story[/b] is pretty good and well thought out, and has some serious twists and turns as it progresses. The characters are interesting and the game does a good job to keep the player guessing. The [b]gameplay[/b] revolves around making decisions on what to upload to "Orwell" (or the computer that connects all the dots) to decide the fate of the citizens that are being investigated. Basically. a text-rich game. Once a decision is made things get set in motion, very quick. During a specific period in the game I had the habit of uploading everything... just be careful what is deemed important! Someone may wrongly get arrested. 

The [b]visuals and graphics[/b] are very easy on the eyes. However, if you're someone who likes when the screen changes every once in a while, this might not totally be up your alley. The game consists of three or so main screens. The first is a headline type screen. This screen lets the player browse the web for interesting information they may come across. The second screen allows the player (working for Orwell) to listen in on live conversations or messages. The third screen is a computer hacking screen in which the player has access to a suspects computer. The game does a good progression to introducing the player to what is going on. The [b]sounds and music[/b] are pretty decent. There are moments in the game where the music will slam and something dramatic will happen. The sounds are alright and there is no live voice to the characters. I imagine being a small developper that can be hard to do, but the text does a decent job delivering a story. I'm not a text sort of gamer (my friend bought me Disco Elysium, I'm sure it's great, but just don't have the patience to play it), this game did catch my attention for a while though.

Why the negative review? If I had to warn my past self, I would advise my past self not to buy it. It's an awesome story, there are cool things that happen, but I feel indifferent to the game. I went down a mystery and I was put on the edge. Not enough for me to really like the game. If you like text based games and something that's a little different on Steam, or even mystery, decisions, and consequences... and especially if this game is on sale, I'd say definitely give it a shot. For me, I had a little fun. That's about it. It is sort of similar to Papers Please; Orwell is a little more linear to one story line. There are branches, but limited. The ending though, was definitely, as some would say, dope.  

This game has a story with a real lesson for the future. Would be interesting to see a new version of this game with more options and new tools to use.

review_text_raw:
[b]Guys!  Perhaps this may come as a shock to some of you but, in case you didn’t know, this game has a bit of an agenda….[/b] 
Ok ok, joking aside I bought Orwell a while back when it fell below my “if I buy this and don’t like it, I won’t feel any great loss” threshold.  It sat in my library untouched until a rainy day when I didn’t feel like getting into anything too involved.  I say this to admit that I went into this with pretty bland expectations.  

I generally view games like this the way I do a book from an unknown author, but that has a premise I like.  I knew going in that the game makers had a point to make and even though it was a point I generally agree with, I was a little wary.  [i]I don’t like being preached at, so I wasn’t sure if I was going to spend the entire game being beat over the head with the rhetoric bat whilst being presented with billboards saying in big bold letters “Hey look, the authors feel very strongly about this” at every turn or if the game would have any merit beyond the political statement.[/i]  [b]I’m very thankful to say that this game was far more than just a tray upon which to serve political and social commentary and it was even very clever in doing so.[/b]

So why did I start out with all that waffle about political commentary?  Because I want to set the tone for how I approached the game and the preconceptions I had going in.  I went into the experience thinking that I pretty much had them figured out and that I would easily be able to see through any “hard choices with lasting consequences” to what the authors were really trying to sell to the player.  And chapter 1 pretty much was just that.  I “knew” they were trying to get me to suspect a particular person and that they wanted me to assume the simple answer so they could jump out from behind the posterized, low-polygon trees and say “Ha!  See how even with all the information at your fingertips you jumped to the wrong conclusion.”  So naturally I did just the opposite.  Purposefully ignoring what I assumed were red-herrings and by the end of chapter 1, I’d almost lost interest figuring that I had it all figured out.  I was delighted, and a bit disappointed, that I was wrong.  

Starting chapter 2, I was actually engaged in the narrative and was now determined not to be caught off-guard again.  I still knew there was a point to it all, but I wasn’t as sure I knew what that point was.  By the end of the game, I knew what was going on, but because I’d fed information to orwell earlier on that seemed harmless at the time, I’d built a profile on some of the characters that was not incorrect but was misrepresentative.  This led to events playing out in a way that I didn’t want and with no way to go back and correct.  I felt duped, but in a good way.  The game had indeed gotten it’s point across, but in a very subtle and engaging way that left me still feeling that I enjoyed the experience.

So let’s sum this up, shall we? 
•	Orwell was well worth the money
•	Gameplay was not nearly as on-rails as I had expected
•	Story was actually very engaging and believable
•	Plot twists did not feel super-contrived simply to force the player to be wrong for the sake of proving a point.  All the plot twists could have been seen coming I think if the user had paid attention to the details and not just focused on what Orwell highlights.
•	The game actually made me think and didn’t preach it’s point smugly from contrived moral high-ground and I appreciated that.  

Here is where I would usually list a few things that could have been improved, but the game is pretty simple and the UI layout is simple and easy to use. What is Orwell ?

Orwell is a game that has managed to make me fully immersed into it, which is something rare, whenever a game makes me Immersed, it automatically makes that game good for me. In concept orwell introduces you into a terrorist situation and you are an hired investigator who must use this new tool called "Orwell" to bring justice to the people involved in this specific situation, the gameplay is very simple, its just clicking and dragging stuff on screen but I'd rather play this and be immersed than play the latest AAA release and fall asleep just 2 hours in, what makes Orwell special is that its a game that every single choice matter, nothing is black and white, for every stuff you do during your investigation, the special traits the supposed terrorist have that you highlight on their profile, to the locations they visited, their personal lives and the people they have a relationship with, all the occurrences that happen during the 5 days the game takes place on, whenever you finish one of the five chapters aka complete a day of investigations theres a lot of consequences, good or not based on what you decided to highlight, since Orwell itself as a program has a imbued browser system and a profile you have to search every corner for information and make sure that youre putting the correct person in jail, theres contradicting information, I for example failed hard on the second day of investigations, I sent the police to the wrong location and because of that a bomb exploded in a public area, killing innocents, something I could prevent and by the end of the game, no matter what you do, we both will always get different endings since theres so many variables at stake and Orwell is such a detailed and immersive game, it makes every decision count. Another thing to add is that the game plays into hard topics that are relevant to our current times and the game does it in such smart way, its not just another pretentious game, its a smart, well-done game. 

Besides the concept Orwell presents a nice soundtrack and a great sense of style, you will always be looking into this program for most of the time but the game uses this environment to show its great artistic design and despite the gameplay being overly simple with the complex way your decisions are taken into consideration, the immersion the game pulls you into and the very interesting way that this game story which Imo was really well done develops, it just becomes a seamless experience, it took me 5 hours to finish and I would gladly replay it again and this time correcting the mistakes I did on my previous playthrough, I think that Orwell is simple an indie masterpiece, it executes its concept with class, add interesting takes into the whole cybersecurity concept and has a simple but engaging gameplay, In my opinion if you want to try something different that stays with you then this game is a must-play, a very memorable and original game.

review_text_raw:
Orwell was an enjoyable, but very flawed game. I struggle with recommending it to anybody, because I can't imagine a particular audience falling in love with it. Gamers looking for a great narrative may find Orwell's offerings lacking, as I have. Gamers who are fans of the works of George Orwell may get what they're looking for, but as a fan myself I find the game's vision lacking. George Orwell's works were a denouncement of totalitarianism, yet his most well-known fictional books were either set in the real world or clearly based on real events and people. Orwell the game instead opts to take place in the wonderful setting of "The Nation" in which "The Party" exercises total control in a fictional world.

While the setting certainly lacks creativity, I was pleased to see that the plot and characters of the game improved as time passed. Orwell places the player as a worker for a state surveillence system looking for the perpetrator of a series of terrorist bombings. The player is tasked with reading various articles, profiles, and personal conversations and sending this information to the authorities within The Nation's government. This sounds more interesting than it plays out, however. In the beginning I was given a suspect who was very clearly not the bomber. I resented my superior for being so brainless for assuming they were responsible. While this suspect inevitably had some connections with people who actually did know more about the bombings, I was frustrated that I had to investigate the suspect in the first place. The gameplay also lacks for imagination. While I enjoyed reading some of the articles and the suspect's internet profiles, conversations, and e-mails, the text that you upload is already pre-determined. It ultimately boils down to a scavenger hunt. There are some choices to make things interesting. Sometimes you will have to chose between two pieces of data to upload to the authorities, as there may be conflicting data. Sometimes this decision is a moral one, and others it's more based around what the player things is more accuracte information. There are even a few times where uploading too much information will lead to unforeseen consequences. Regardless, for the most part the gameplay is very linear and will ultimately turn off many gamers. The gameplay gets more interesting in the final chapter when the uploads you can make are limited and the pressure is heightened, yet this improvement comes too little, too late.

Orwell is a game I want to love and there are moments of quality within. The general conclusion to the story was pulled off fairly well and there are consequences for chocies that many probably would not have anticipated being held accountable for. The characters and their interactions amongst each other are far more engaging than the uncreative setting. I hope for the sequel the developers be more bold with their setting, their message, and ultimately make the gameplay more interesting for a wider audience.

review_text_raw:
[h1]Preface[/h1]
This review is being written before the conclusion of the game in episode five. I've played through the first four episodes a couple times exploring different outcomes, however, as episode five is not out yet I'm not able to comment on the totallity of the story.

[h1]The Machine[/h1]
[b][i]Orwell[/i][/b] has a very close [url=http://www.cbs.com/shows/person_of_interest/]Person of Interest[/url] vibe. The government of the fictitious country has obtained a Machine, or System, that surveils the populous gathering information however it does not act on the gathered information. The idea of the game is that the system, aptly named [b][i]Orwell[/i][/b], isn't able to decern human subtlety, sarcasim, or deciet. As such, the fictious government has [b]outsourced[/b] the task of resolving conflicts in the data, and identifying what is relevant and what is not. You as the player take on this role as an outsider to the country, tasked with sifting through the data that [b][i]Orwell[/i][/b] gives you access to inorder to identify person(s) of interest. This is a role somewhat like [i]Person of Interest[/i]'s Harold Finch.

[h1]What [i]Orwell[/i] Is Not[/h1]
I've seen several complaints that the game isn't challenging enough, many comparing it to several "hacker simulators" such as [b][i]Hacknet[/i][/b] or [b][i]UPLINK[/i][/b]. On the surface the concept might seem somewhat similar to games such as these, however, this is not what [b][i]Orwell[/i][/b] is. In this game you are not doing any "hacking" or "cracking", that is [b][i]Orwell[/i][/b]'s job. You are more of a data analyst telling a hacker, that happens to be a computer system, what data is relevant and linked to certian people. Treating it in the same vein as other "hacker simulators" isn't fair to the game and if that is what you are expecting, you will be dissapointed.

[h1]What [i]Orwell[/i] Is[/h1]
So if [b][i]Orwell[/i][/b] isn't a "hacker simulator" what is it? I've also seen the categorization as a "visual novel" which is much closer to what this game is. The game play is reminiscent of [url=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Choose_Your_Own_Adventure]Choose Your Own Adventure[/url] books some of you might have read as a child. As such, the outcomes that occur in the game depend on what data you choose to "flag" or "link" to someone as relevant. This process will estabilsh relationships between persons of interest that may uncover new motivations, or might change the context of the data you have available. The game is about you being the guiding hand for a surveillance system tasked with preventing & solving crime.

[h1]Pros[/h1]
[list]
    [*]Interesting visual style
    [*]Enjoyable storyline that feels very linear (as it should), but leaves you with a sprinkling of "what if" moments where you feel things could have been different.
    [*]Fairly Intuitive gameplay.
[/list]

[h1]Cons[/h1]
[list]
    [*]Somewhat short, although there is some replay value if you want to try to achieve different outcomes from prior play through(s)
    [*]You aren't able to link data to someone until [b][i]Orwell[/i][/b] identifies it as potentially relevant.
    [*]You aren't able to revise or change "known" data based on new information
    [*]You aren't able to alter "data conflicts" if you find additional information
    [*]No "Save Game" system, uses the idea of profiles instead to allow for differing play throughs
[/list]

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
The game is a fun and enjoyable experience if you do not have unrealistic expectations of what the game is and what the gameplay is like. It offers an interesting and thought provoking social commentary on the age of information technology that we live in. The game presents the idea of freedom & privacy -vs- surveillance & security in an interesting and fairly balanced way. If you actually think about what you are doing moment-by-moment in the game, you will likely find yourself re-evaluating your thoughts on these topics. That isn't to say this game is going to challenge your views or change your mind, simply that you will likely find yourself thinking about these topics and why you hold your views on these topics.

If you enjoy naritive driven experiences this game will likey fit well in your games library. While there are some things the game could certianly do better I didn't find these issues to detract significantly from the games main draw for me, it's story & premise. I would like to see the game updated with some sort of "Save Game" system that would allow you to "branch off" after each chapter within a single profile. This would make exploring different outcomes easier, howerver, I also can see that this goes against the linear nature of the games concept. The game strives to make you feel like you are participating in the events, that are time bound and as such linear in nature, which have consequences.

Overall I'm enjoying the game and would recommend it to those who enjoy adventure games, visual novels, and mysteries. This isn't really a problem/puzzle solving game (like a "hacker simulator") so if that is what you are looking for you may wish to pass on this game. I definitely recommend it for what it is and I'm really looking forward to the culmination of these events in episode five.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
This is a difficult one! The premise and the story are both quite complicated and intelligently woven. However, the execution is less so. This game suffers from the very same type of problems that LA Noire did: how to make a detective/analysis game without too little or too much handholding.

The idea of the investigative software is quite well-written; and depending on your ending, has a lot of payoffs. But the fact that the software pinpoints what it thinks is important and relevant kinda breaks the realism and limits a lot of your options. A lot of times, decisions that you make won't have the intended consequences and not because "life is complicated" or "shit happens" but because that's now how you linguistically interpreted the data. And that is the limitation of every game that has attempted to use language as a mechanic. There are still too many unknowns and interpretations to be able to identify and script every possible `effect` after you've set a `cause`.


Of course, there's no undo or rollback so you have to keep going with what you've done so far. The concept of `conflicting info` is also weird and unrealistic. Sometimes, it warns you that this info conflicts with some other info that you haven't even loaded or read. How does the software know that?! I realize that this aspect of analysis needs to be "gamefied" but that's where this game shows its greatest weakness. It's as if the software is already run by an AI and you just need to answer a few multiple choice questions here and there.

There's also a number of annoying UI issues like notifications. I kept gettings notifications for new or unread articles when I had accessed them and read them numerous times. Same with the datachunk notification. And when you're hunting for something specific towards the end of the game, and you have a ton of data, those icons can get downright annoying and misleading forcing you to skim and scroll through heaps of useless articles.

Still, the game and the story have a lot to say about our current society and it's definitely worth a replay for things you might have missed the first time. Not to mention that it has multiple endings.

The music's quite good too!

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell is a game where you step into the shoes of an "Investigator"; an individual specially chosen outside of the dystopian-like nation simply titled "The Nation" to interact with a big-brother type software that allows you to track and keep tabs on every single person in The Nation. You take control of yourself, your name, your info, you. You've been specially chosen for reasons unknown to yourself or anyone else, per the exception of a secretive few, to be hired at Orwell. Your new "Adviser", Symes, is going to show you the ropes of international and domestic espionage, only this time, you aren't taking down super villians or having a martini "shaken, not stirred" as per the classic spy movie or game, Orwell instead hits close to home....a little too close.

Orwell is a Story Rich, Dystopian, "Choices Matter" Indie game made by Osmotic Studios where you "Investigate the lives of citizens to find those responsible for a series of terror attacks. Information from the internet, personal communications and private files are all accessible to you. But, be warned, the information you supply will have consequences.". When Osmotic says that choices matter, they really do. You feel as if you're truly in this dystopian world, helping, or harming, The Nation's citizens. You get to look through countless web pages, trace and listen to countless phone calls, emails, text message and otherwise, even hack into citizen's computers or mobile phones to gain access to information stored on there, such as browsing history, photos, files, and even deleted files. 

For an example (spoiler free); You will be investigating certain citizens, and obviously need to find certain clues about them, their age, phone number, email address, face id, street info, parents, siblings, workplace, links to them from other sources, and you can even go as far as finding medical info from The Nation's hospitals. 

Now let's say I have a citizen I'm investigating, I can start with their relative name, go from there to their social media pages, find out their DOB, address, friends, maybe even mobile number. let's say I need to (or want to) take it further, I begin to suspect they're somehow a threat to The Nation. I can do a little research, Get in contact with friends, trace their calls and emails,  find out information that was never meant to be seen by hacking their computer by getting their PSI address or their IP address, or find ways into their workplace, or even goof off and research their background, what their favourite colour is, or who they're in a relationship with.

Orwell does an amazing job at immersing the investigator (you) into dystopian earth, into The Nation and it's surrounding countries, the citizens who inhabit them and even smaller things like a simple webpage for a local university or a humanitarian organization. Once I started the game, I honestly did not have high expectations nor did I think it was going to be something i was going to enjoy, since it just didn't look or seem like the type of game or genre that i liked, but once i started investigating and learning more about this country, it's citizens and the lore about this world I simply couldn't put it down. I played all the way through, read tons of webpages, information, emails and texts.

That being said, the game is roughly 3-4 hours long, maybe shorter if you (somehow) speedrun it, but if you really want to get immersed into this game world then it can take a lot longer.

[i] And that's not neccesarily a bad thing. [/i]

This is one of a only video game worlds and lore that I genuinly became interested in and invested in as time went on, it truly made me feel like I was impacting the citizens and world around me, mainly because I actually was.

One of the reasons this game resonated with me so much (and one of the reasons I am recommending it) is because in reality, this is not very dystopian. Things like this very well happen in real life and seem so real it's almost disturbing. The amount of dialogue in this game is astonishing, from everything to simple text messages to elaborate corporate emails, everything seems completely geniune, and feels that way too.

Orwell is a masterpeice at storytelling and really making the player truly become immersed and feel like there are consequences. Season 2 of Orwell is coming out sometime soon, and I WILL DEFINETLY be purchasing this game. I highly recommend this game to anyone who likes immersive game worlds, spy type games, choice matter games, or just mind-f*ck type games. Absolute great game. 10/10

Oh yeah, this game also takes place in 2017
[i] Weird, huh? [/i]

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1]Description[/h1]

Orwell is a visual novel that puts you in the shoes of a Big Brother employee: you are tasked with spying on people and uploading to the system anything suspicious. Unlike most visual novels, you are not presented here with walls of text followed by lists of choices. Rather, your interaction with the game and its unfolding story goes solely through the gimmick of uploading the data chunks you find (or not). By picking among conflicting data chunks or by choosing not to upload some sensitive information, you impact the story in small and big ways.

[h1]Pros[/h1]
[list]
[*] Fresh interaction gimmick that goes very well with the theme
[*] Credible writing with many characters each having their own style of speech
[*] Interesting choices going WAY beyond the good/bad dichotomy
[*] Decent art style
[*] Fair amount of consequences to choices made, though the game remains linear
[/list]

[h1]Cons[/h1]
[list]
[*] Notification system takes some getting used to ([spoiler]the system will sometimes find old information suddenly relevant, requiring you to regularly browse through the lists of documents to make sure no red star has popped[/spoiler])
[*] Because all chats and phone calls are delivered sloooooowly (and I found no way to speed them up), replaying the game to get the achievements or test other choices is a bit of a chore
[*] Political messages are (very) thinly veiled and might annoy (or even anger?) some players
[/list]

[h1]Verdict[/h1]

Do you hate it when someone tries to convey a political message artistically and ends up as subtle as a bull in a china shop? If so, stay away from this game. You're going to hate it.

Still here? OK, here's an idea: put yourself in the shoes of an orwellian enforcer and imagine the consequences of government trampling all over freedom, privacy and presumption of innocence.

Interested? Then try Orwell. Go in expecting a fresh visual novel and a politically charged (to the point of being heavy-handed at times) thought experiment. There is much to like.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
This is not a game. It's more like a fancy choose your own adventure book. There is a limited number of ways that the story completes, and other than a few important decision points your actions have little consequence to how the story plays out. See the  Wikipedia page if you want to know the story before hand.  

I did not enjoy this experience, i did not find it fun, and here are my main complaints:

1) You spend all of your  time sifting through emails and texts looking for important information or data chunks. This is not a challenge because the information is highlighted for you. To make matters  even dumber, the specific emails, texts, etc are marked with an icon to show you which ones have the important information you need to act on.

2) The important decision points in the game are also highlighted in bright yellow as conflicting data chunks. You have to choose which one Orwell (the computer) will consider as fact. Often times you have to do this without any way of knowing the actual truth, but the implications of the choices are always glaringly obvious. 

3) There are data chunks that have to be given to Orwell for the story to progress, even if you don't  want to provide it. This is the one thing the ruined the experience for me, and made it obvious that the program is leading you by the nose and you have no real control. I get it. You can't read a book from the middle out, and in a "game" that is basically just a click-through-story you have to proceed in the order the author intends. All the important information has to be in place for the story to make sense. 

Lastly, and this is a minor quibble, but I also take issue with the name of this "game". Orwell is a stupidly ironic name. George Orwell was an opponent of totalitarianism, not it's champion. Perhaps a better literary subject to steal would have been Colossus (Dennis Feltham Jones). At least that Colossus was a computer.
